source: seed (original case written for this app)
title: Ayurvedic skincare brand: 3x in three years
opening: Our client is Vanaspa, a digital-first Ayurvedic skincare brand. It did about ₹120 crore of revenue last year and its investors want it to reach about ₹360 crore within three years, ahead of a possible IPO. The founders have asked us how they should get there.
client_context: Founded 2018. Hero products: a kumkumadi face oil and an ubtan face wash. Sells through its own website, marketplaces (Amazon, Nykaa) and a small offline pilot. Contribution-margin positive but EBITDA negative due to marketing spend.
objective: Identify the growth levers and a plan to reach ~₹360 crore revenue in three years without destroying unit economics.

clarifications.answer: Investors want growth, but they will not fund a plan in which marketing spend grows faster than revenue. The company should reach EBITDA break-even by year three.
About 40 SKUs; the top 5 hero products are ~65% of revenue. Face care is the core category.
India only. About 70% of revenue comes from the top 8 metros.

data.label: Revenue by channel, last year
data.content: Own website ₹50 cr, marketplaces ₹52 cr, offline pilot ₹18 cr (about 200 modern-trade and pharmacy doors).
data.release_when: Candidate asks for revenue split by channel.

data.label: Customer metrics
data.content: About 12 lakh active customers; average order value ₹700; ~1.43 orders per customer per year. 12-month repeat rate is 22%; category leaders are around 40%.
data.release_when: Candidate breaks revenue into customers × frequency × order value, or asks about retention/repeat.

data.label: Digital acquisition cost trend
data.content: Blended customer acquisition cost (CAC) on digital rose from ₹450 two years ago to ₹900 now. First-order contribution margin is about ₹280.
data.release_when: Candidate asks about marketing efficiency, CAC, or scaling digital acquisition.

data.label: Offline opportunity
data.content: The offline pilot doors average about ₹9 lakh revenue per door per year at ~25% contribution after trade margins, with no customer acquisition cost. There are roughly 8,000 relevant modern-trade and premium-pharmacy doors in the top 30 cities. New doors typically do about two-thirds of pilot productivity.
data.release_when: Candidate asks about offline/retail expansion or the offline pilot.

exhibits.title: Channel economics, last year
exhibits.release_when: Candidate asks to compare channels or asks where growth has come from.
takeaways: The website is the least profitable after marketing and slowest-growing: digital acquisition is saturating.
Offline has the best contribution and fastest growth, but from a small base.
Repeat rates are low, so retention is a lever.

quant.question: What would it take to add ₹240 cr purely through digital acquisition?
quant.solution: Revenue per active customer ≈ ₹700 × 1.43 ≈ ₹1,000/yr → need ~24 lakh more active customers. At CAC ₹900 that is ~₹216 cr of acquisition spend before churn (more, given 22% repeat), which is more than current revenue. Not viable under the marketing constraint.
quant.answer: ~24 lakh more customers and ₹200+ cr of acquisition spend: not viable

quant.question: Size the offline lever.
quant.solution: ~2,500 doors × ₹6 lakh (two-thirds of ₹9 lakh) ≈ ₹150 cr in three years.

quant.question: Size the retention lever.
quant.solution: Raising orders per customer from 1.43 to ~1.8 (repeat 22% → ~35%) on a base of ~15-18 lakh customers at ₹700 AOV adds roughly ₹40-50 cr.

analytical_paths: Revenue = customers × frequency × AOV, by channel → acquisition is saturated (CAC doubled) → retention and offline are the capital-efficient levers → size each → plan to ₹360 cr.
Growth levers tree: core (penetration, frequency, pricing) vs adjacencies (new categories, channels, geographies, inorganic), then prioritised using the channel economics.
key_insights: Digital acquisition has hit diminishing returns (CAC doubled; website margin after marketing is only 4%), so 'more of the same' cannot deliver 3x under the constraint.
Offline modern trade and pharmacies are the largest capital-efficient lever (~₹150 cr).
Retention (repeat 22% vs 40% benchmark) is a cheap lever worth ~₹40-50 cr.
reference_solution: Clarify the constraint (no marketing-led growth). Break revenue into customers × frequency × AOV by channel. The channel exhibit shows digital is saturating and offline has the best economics. Sizing: offline ~₹150 cr (2,500 doors × ₹6 lakh), retention ~₹40-50 cr, marketplace growth and selective digital ~₹30-40 cr, and product extensions (e.g. body care from hero ingredients) ~₹20-30 cr. That gets to ~₹360 cr. Sequence: retention quick wins in year 1, offline scale-up years 1-3, adjacencies year 2+.
alternative_approaches: An Ansoff-style view (penetration/product/market/diversification) is acceptable if the candidate prioritises with the economics instead of listing it.
Inorganic growth (acquiring a complementary brand) is a valid option to discuss, especially given IPO timing, but should be tested against capital availability.
recommendation: Pursue a capital-efficient growth plan: (1) scale offline to ~2,500 modern-trade/pharmacy doors (~₹150 cr), with a distributor model and planograms for hero SKUs; (2) fix retention with regimen-based bundles, subscriptions and CRM (~₹40-50 cr); (3) keep digital acquisition at efficient CAC only; (4) extend hero ingredients into adjacent categories (~₹20-30 cr). Risks: offline working capital and returns, channel price conflict with marketplaces, and brand dilution. Next steps: pilot distributor model in 3 cities, and test retention levers on existing cohorts.
interviewer_notes: Push candidates who say 'increase marketing' to confront the CAC data and the constraint.
A strong candidate adds up the levers to check they reach ₹360 cr.
common_pitfalls: Listing growth options without sizing them.
Forgetting to check that the levers add up to the target.
learning_objective: Build a growth plan that prioritises levers by economics and sizes them against a target.

source: seed (original case written for this app)
title: Quick commerce: taking the model to Tier-2 India
opening: Our client is ZipKart, a quick-commerce company delivering groceries in 10-15 minutes in 8 metro cities. It is profitable at the dark-store level in the metros. The board wants to enter 20 Tier-2 cities such as Indore, Nagpur, Coimbatore and Lucknow next year. Should they, and if so, how?
client_context: ~600 dark stores in metros. Well funded. A competitor has announced Tier-2 plans. ZipKart ran a 3-month pilot with 4 dark stores in Indore.
objective: Decide whether and how to enter Tier-2 cities profitably. The board wants each dark store to break even within 12 months of launch.

clarifications.answer: Each dark store should reach break-even at the contribution-after-store-costs level within 12 months.
ZipKart earns a margin of about 18% on what it sells, plus a small delivery fee. Costs are riders, packaging and payment per order, plus the fixed costs of running each dark store.
One competitor has announced Tier-2 plans but has launched in only 2 cities so far. Local kiranas already offer phone ordering and home delivery in many neighbourhoods.

data.label: Market demand signals
data.content: Target cities have 10-40 lakh people each. App downloads from these cities are already ~6% of the national base. Urban household spend on groceries is ~70% of metro levels.
data.release_when: Candidate asks about market size, demand or customer interest.

data.label: Dark-store fixed costs
data.content: Metro dark store: ~₹8 lakh per month (rent ₹2.5 lakh, staff ₹4 lakh, other ₹1.5 lakh). Tier-2 dark store: ~₹5.5 lakh per month.
data.release_when: Candidate asks about store-level costs, setup or break-even.

data.label: Indore pilot demand
data.content: The Indore pilot stores are at ~220 orders/day after 3 months and the trend suggests ~350 orders/day at maturity.
data.release_when: Candidate asks about expected order volumes or pilot results.

data.label: Levers tested in pilot
data.content: Adding electronics accessories, pharmacy and gifting raised AOV in one pilot store by about 15%. A 25-30 minute promise (instead of 10-15) lets one store serve roughly 1.6x the catchment area.
data.release_when: Candidate asks how to improve unit economics, AOV, or density.

exhibits.title: Per-order economics: metro vs Indore pilot (₹ per order)
exhibits.release_when: Candidate asks about unit economics, per-order profitability or contribution.
takeaways: Tier-2 contribution per order is ~₹31 vs ₹55 in metros, mainly because AOV is ~30% lower.
Lower rider cost only partly offsets the lower AOV.

quant.question: Break-even orders per day for a Tier-2 dark store
quant.solution: Fixed cost ₹5.5 lakh/month ≈ ₹18,300/day. Contribution ₹31/order → ~590 orders/day (≈583 with ₹31.4). Metro: ₹8 lakh/month ≈ ₹26,700/day ÷ ₹55 ≈ 485 orders/day.
quant.answer: ~580-590 orders/day in Tier-2 vs ~485 in metros

quant.question: Gap at expected maturity
quant.solution: Expected 350 orders/day vs break-even ~585 → about 60% of break-even. Loss ≈ (585-350) × ₹31 ≈ ₹7,300/day ≈ ₹2.2 lakh per store per month.
quant.answer: Each store runs at ~60% of break-even volume, losing roughly ₹2 lakh a month

analytical_paths: Market attractiveness → can we win → economics. The economics show the standard model doesn't break even, which reframes the entry question into 'what model works'.
Hypothesis-first: 'Tier-2 demand exists, but lower AOV and density break the dark-store unit economics' → test with per-order economics and break-even.
key_insights: Demand exists; the issue is unit economics. Tier-2 contribution per order is ~₹31 vs ₹55 in metros, driven by AOV.
Break-even needs ~585 orders/day but mature stores reach ~350, so a straight copy of the metro model fails the board's criterion.
Entry is viable only with a modified model: larger catchment (longer promise), higher-AOV assortment, and fewer, bigger cities first.
reference_solution: Market entry reframed as a unit-economics problem. Check market attractiveness (it exists), then per-order and store economics: contribution ₹31/order × expected 350 orders/day doesn't cover ₹18,300/day of fixed costs (break-even ~585). Levers: AOV +15% (assortment) → contribution ~₹42 (margin 0.18 × 437 ≈ 79 + 10 - 35 - 12 ≈ ₹42); a 1.6x catchment raises orders to ~560 → ~₹23,500/day contribution vs ₹18,300 fixed cost, so the store breaks even. Recommend a staged entry: 4-5 largest Tier-2 cities with the modified model, then expand based on store-level break-even.
alternative_approaches: Asset-light entry: partner with local kiranas or supermarkets as fulfilment points instead of dark stores.
Acquisition of a regional grocery delivery player, if one exists, as a way to buy density.
recommendation: Don't roll out the metro model to 20 cities. Enter the 4-5 largest Tier-2 cities with a modified model: a 25-30 minute promise to widen catchments, and an assortment that adds higher-AOV categories. The pilot data suggest this reaches break-even (~₹42 × ~560 orders ≈ ₹23.5k/day vs ₹18.3k fixed). Gate further expansion on store-level break-even within 12 months. Risks: the competitor moving first, customer acceptance of a slower promise, and kirana responses. Next steps: run the modified model in 2 Indore stores for 8 weeks.
interviewer_notes: Candidates who spend most of the time on market size miss the point; steer only via probes.
Good candidates compute break-even and compare it with expected volume unprompted.
common_pitfalls: Treating it as a pure market attractiveness exercise.
Saying 'enter because the competitor is entering'.
Not converting monthly fixed cost to daily before dividing.
learning_objective: Recognise when a market-entry question turns on unit economics, and design the entry model around break-even.

title: Pro kabaddi franchise: growing revenue
opening: Our client owns a professional kabaddi franchise based in Jaipur. Revenue is about ₹60 crore a year and the owner wants to grow it by 50% in two years. How would you think about it?
client_context: League revenues are shared centrally (media rights), plus franchise-level sponsorship, ticketing and merchandise. Season lasts ~3 months; home games are ~11 matches.
objective: Find the most promising ways to grow franchise revenue by ~₹30 crore in two years.

clarifications.answer: Central media-rights share ₹35 cr (fixed by the league), sponsorships ₹18 cr, ticketing ₹4 cr, merchandise & other ₹3 cr.
Home arena seats ~4,500; average occupancy ~70%; average ticket ~₹800.
~2.5 million social followers, mostly Rajasthan and Haryana; the team finished in the top 4 last season.

data.label: Sponsorship benchmark
data.content: Top franchises in the league earn ₹30-35 cr in sponsorship; they sell 12-15 sponsor slots (jersey front, back, sleeves, arena, digital), while the client sells 7.
data.release_when: Candidate asks about sponsorship, benchmarks or inventory.

data.label: Off-season engagement
data.content: The franchise runs no off-season events. Two other franchises run youth academies and a state-level league that generate ₹4-6 cr each in fees and sponsorship.
data.release_when: Candidate asks about off-season/year-round revenue or community/academy ideas.

quant.question: Ticketing upside
quant.solution: 11 games × 4,500 × 70% × ₹800 ≈ ₹2.8 cr (reported ₹4 cr includes premium seats/boxes). Even at 100% occupancy and +25% price, ticketing adds only ~₹2-3 cr.

analytical_paths: Split revenue into fixed (central media) and controllable streams → ticketing is capped by capacity → sponsorship inventory gap vs peers is the biggest lever → off-season properties as a second lever.
Fan-engagement lens: grow fan base → monetise via sponsors, merchandise, events.
key_insights: ₹35 cr of ₹60 cr is fixed central revenue, so the 50% growth must come from ~₹25 cr of controllable revenue, i.e. more than doubling it.
Ticketing is capacity-capped (a few crore at most); sponsorship inventory (7 vs 12-15 slots) is the main lever (~₹12-15 cr).
Year-round properties (academy, state league) are the second lever (~₹5 cr).
reference_solution: Separate fixed and controllable revenue. Ticketing is capacity-constrained. Sponsorship is under-monetised versus top franchises: expanding inventory (digital, arena, sleeves) and packaging it with content could add ₹12-15 cr. Launch year-round properties (academy, state league, content) for ~₹5 cr, and build merchandise with the fan base for ~₹2-4 cr. Reaching +₹30 cr is stretched; ~₹20-25 cr is realistic in two years.
alternative_approaches: A fan-lifecycle approach (acquire, engage, monetise) is valid if it gets to the sponsorship lever.
Pushing back on the target (+50% is unrealistic given the fixed central share) is good business judgment.
recommendation: Focus on sponsorship inventory expansion (+₹12-15 cr) and year-round properties (+~₹5 cr), plus merchandise; tell the owner that +₹20-25 cr is realistic in two years and +₹30 cr needs a stronger on-field brand or a second arena market. Risks: sponsor demand depends on team performance and viewership.
interviewer_notes: Unfamiliar industry: reward first-principles reasoning about how a franchise makes money.
common_pitfalls: Spending time on ticket pricing, which is capped.
learning_objective: Separate controllable from fixed revenue and prioritise levers by size in an unfamiliar industry.
